newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's tax plan curbs loopholes, aids families.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's tax plan curbs loopholes, aids families.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's budget proposed cuts in federal income taxes worth $98 billion for families over five years, according to White House documents obtained by reporters on Wednesday.

Much of the tax cut would be paid for by $76 billion in increases on a host of different taxes paid by corporations and investors, extensions of excise taxes and new fees for government services. Separately, the government would raise $36 billion over five years by selling broadcast spectrum.

The tax proposals were largely expected by the Republican-controlled Congress, which hopes to negotiate broader tax relief, including a deep reduction in the capital gains tax paid on investment profits. They have some reason for hope in this area, since the president has said he is not as tied to capital gains taxes as are other Democrats.

Clinton will also seek tax relief for families through a $500 per child tax credit, an idea Republicans have also put on the table. As part of the improvements in education Clinton announced to the nation on Tuesday night, he asked for a $1,500 tax credit or a $10,000 deduction for tuition.

His capital gains tax relief centres on a relatively slight tax break for homeowners which would raise the amount of profit that can be excluded from taxation upon resale. At present people under 55 can roll over gains into a higher priced home, and can exclude $250,000 from tax if they sell after age 55.
Several controversial tax breaks for investors would be tightened or closed by his proposal.

Investors, particularly those holding mutual funds, would be forced to use the average price of a stock when figuring gains or losses upon sale, called "average cost basis." Currently investors have more flexibility in calculating for tax purposes the sale price of their stocks.

Another profitable tax break for investors, called "selling short against the box," would be eliminated in Clinton's plan. Rather than selling stock that is owned, investors are able to sell identical stock they have borrowed with their own stock used as collateral. His plan also changed rules on taxation of inventory and recommended the replacement of sales source rules with activity-based rules, a break worth $7.5 billion over five years.

As in last year's White House budget, the plan would also restrict the interest deductions companies get from investments in tax-exempt bonds and planned to limit the dividends-received deduction tax break.
In addition, congressional staff said Treasury officials informed them Clinton would seek to repeal the subsidy that multinational companies receive for exports to foreign units.
The Senate Finance Committee this week approved an extension until September of the 10 percent airline ticket tax, one of the excise taxes the president sought to extend.
He also recommended extension of the oil spill excise tax.
